opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is just leverage. When I'm doing research myself, I'm one person with a fixed number of hours, and I'm limited by my own ideas, my own taste, my own blind spots. But when I'm mentoring or supervising, I can spend maybe an hour a week with someone and meaningfully change the direction of a project they'll put forty hours into. If I can help them avoid a dead end, or notice that the interesting thing is actually over *here*, that's a pretty enormous multiplier on my time.

And I think mechanistic interpretability in particular is a field where this matters a lot. It's young, it's small, and there's a huge amount of low-hanging fruit, but there's also a lot of tacit knowledge that isn't written down anywhere. Things like: how do you tell when a result is real versus when you've fooled yourself? When should you give up on a direction? How do you pick a problem that's tractable but still actually important? A lot of that you only really learn by doing research next to someone who's made those mistakes before. So I feel like one of the most useful things I can do is help transmit that, and help grow the number of people who can do good work here.

There's also a more selfish answer, which is that I just find it really fun. I have far more ideas than I could ever personally execute on, and it's genuinely delightful to throw out a half-baked thought and then watch a talented person turn it into something real, often something much better than what I'd imagined. And I get exposure to way more projects than I would otherwise, which makes me a better researcher too. I'm constantly learning from the people I mentor.

I'll add that I didn't necessarily expect to enjoy it this much. I think there's a common assumption that "real" research is the hands-on coding and experiments, and that management is this thing you get pulled into. But I've come to think that for someone at my stage, being a good mentor and helping set research direction is probably where a lot of my comparative advantage lies, and I find that genuinely satisfying rather than a sacrifice.

r001.rationale: He describes mentoring and supervision as leverage: an hour of guidance can meaningfully redirect a researcher’s much larger project effort, multiplying his impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a few different things going on here. The first is just that I care a lot about the problem. I think interpretability is one of the more promising things we can be doing for alignment, and I want a lot of good work to happen in it. And at some point you realise that there's only so much you personally can do. If I'm sitting there doing research myself, I'm one person. But if I'm managing a team of, say, eight or ten really strong researchers, and I can make each of them meaningfully more effective — help them pick better problems, avoid dead ends I've already hit, give feedback that turns a mediocre project into a great one — then the amount of research that happens as a result of my existing is just a lot larger. That's basically the multiplier argument, and I find it pretty compelling.

The second thing, which I think people underrate, is that I actually find it really fun. I get a lot of enjoyment out of mentoring. There's something very satisfying about watching someone go from "I don't really know how to do research" to "I'm producing work that I think is genuinely good," and knowing you had some role in that. I've done quite a lot of that through things like MATS, and it's consistently been one of the most rewarding things I do.

And then the third thing is a bit more about my particular strengths. I think I have decent research taste — I'm reasonably good at looking at a direction and going "that's probably not going to work" or "that's interesting, but the real question is this other thing." And research taste is, I think, one of the main things that's actually scarce. Lots of people can execute on a well-specified problem. Far fewer people are good at figuring out which problems are worth working on in the first place. If that's a comparative advantage I have, then the way to make the most of it is to spread it across many projects rather than just my own.

I'll be honest that it's also a trade-off. There's a part of me that misses just sitting down for a week and getting my hands dirty with a model and figuring something out. Management means a lot of my time is meetings and reviewing documents and thinking about people. But I think on net it's clearly the right call for me right now, and I don't think I'd want it any other way.

r001.rationale: He says supervising a team can make each researcher more effective and increase the amount of research produced, calling this the “multiplier argument.”

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that I really enjoy helping someone become a better researcher. Someone comes in with a vague idea, and you help them turn it into a concrete question, figure out what experiment would actually teach them something, and notice when the results don’t support the story they wanted to tell. Seeing them get better at that—and increasingly do it without your help—is really satisfying.

There’s also the leverage. If I have useful research taste or intuitions about which problems are promising, doing everything myself is only one way to use that. Helping several people choose better directions can potentially accomplish a lot more. And I get to think about a wider range of interesting problems, which is just fun.

The balance I find interesting is giving enough guidance that someone isn’t stuck and miserable, while leaving enough room for them to develop their own judgment. You want to help them become an independent researcher.

r001.rationale: He says his research taste can help several people choose better directions, potentially accomplishing more than doing everything himself, and describes helping them become better, more independent researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is that I really enjoy helping people get better at research. There’s something very satisfying about working with someone who has good ideas but hasn’t yet developed the judgment to turn them into a tractable project, and helping them figure out what question they’re actually trying to answer, what experiment would be informative, and when to move on.

And I enjoy the intellectual variety. If I’m doing a project myself, I have to spend a lot of time getting all the details to work. As a supervisor, I can engage with several different projects, help with the parts where I have something useful to contribute, and learn from what people discover.

There’s also a multiplier effect that appeals to me. Helping someone become a more independent researcher can matter beyond whatever project we happen to be working on together. Ideally, they come away better able to choose good problems and make progress without me.

r001.rationale: He says helping someone become a more independent researcher can have impact beyond their shared project, clearly describing supervision as a way to multiply his impact.
